name: F.P. Journe
tagline: Invenit et Fecit: one man's inventions, built in 18k gold movements in Geneva
summary: F.P. Journe is the Geneva manufacture of French-born watchmaker François-Paul Journe, famed for resonance chronometers, remontoir tourbillons and solid rose-gold movements. With under a thousand watches a year and huge collector demand, it is widely regarded as the most successful independent of its generation.
history:
François-Paul Journe was born in Marseille in 1957 and trained at the Paris watchmaking school before working in his uncle's restoration workshop. There he built his first tourbillon pocket watch by hand, and through the 1980s and early 1990s he made unique pocket watches and developed movements for other houses from his own workshop, later based in Geneva.

In 1999 he launched watches under his own name with the Tourbillon Souverain, a wristwatch tourbillon with a constant-force remontoir. It was followed in 2000 by the Chronomètre à Résonance, the first serially produced wristwatch using two balances that fall into acoustic resonance. The Octa automatic platform, with a 120-hour reserve, spawned a family of complications. From 2004 the brand switched to movements made entirely in 18k rose gold, a signature that remains unique among manufactures. Journe signs his dials 'Invenit et Fecit' - invented and made.

The company is still controlled by Journe, but in 2018 Chanel acquired a 20% minority stake in Montres Journe SA, pledging to preserve its independence. Collections now span the Classique line (Chronomètre Bleu, Résonance, Tourbillon Souverain, Astronomic Souveraine), the sporty LineSport, the Octa family, and the quartz-powered Élégante with its motion-sensing standby mode.

The brand makes under a thousand watches a year from its Geneva manufacture and its own case and dial suppliers, sells primarily through its own boutiques, and its pieces regularly trade well above retail at auction, where unique and early pieces have fetched millions.

name: H. Moser & Cie
tagline: Very rare Schaffhausen manufacture known for fumé dials and deadpan provocation
summary: H. Moser & Cie is a revived 19th-century house based in Neuhausen am Rheinfall, making in-house movements and hairsprings. Under the Meylan family it became famous for minimalist 'Concept' fumé dials, Vantablack pieces and satirical stunts.
history:
Heinrich Moser, a watchmaker's son from Schaffhausen, founded his firm in St Petersburg in 1828, selling high-quality pocket watches across the Russian Empire. He returned to Schaffhausen a wealthy industrialist, built hydraulic infrastructure on the Rhine and helped found the city's industrial base, while production for the Russian market continued from Le Locle.

After the 1917 revolution the Russian business was nationalised, and the Swiss operations passed through several hands before the name went dormant in the late 20th century. In 2005 the brand was revived in Schaffhausen by a group including Moser's great-grandson Roger Nicholas Balsiger and Dr. Jürgen Lange, launching with in-house calibres and an interchangeable escapement module. Sister company Precision Engineering AG gave Moser the rare ability to make its own hairsprings.

In 2012 the Meylan family's MELB Holding took over, and Edouard Meylan became CEO in 2013. Moser adopted the slogan 'Very Rare', stripped logos off many dials, and turned its signature gradient fumé dials into the brand's calling card. It also courted attention with provocative pieces - the Swiss Mad watch with a case partly made of Vacherin cheese, the Swiss Alp Watch mocking the Apple Watch, and the first Vantablack dials.

Today Moser produces a few thousand watches a year from Neuhausen am Rheinfall across the Endeavour, Pioneer, Streamliner and Heritage collections, and has become one of the best-known 'accessible' independents.

name: MB&F
tagline: Maximilian Büsser & Friends: kinetic sculptures that happen to tell time
summary: MB&F is a Geneva-based 'horological concept laboratory' founded by Maximilian Büsser in 2005, creating Horological Machines inspired by sci-fi, animals and machines alongside the more classical Legacy Machines. It collaborates with independent watchmakers and designers, and Chanel took a 25% stake in 2024.
history:
Maximilian Büsser spent seven years at Jaeger-LeCoultre and then ran Harry Winston's watch division, where he created the Opus series of collaborations with independent watchmakers. In 2005 he left to found MB&F - Maximilian Büsser & Friends - an 'artistic and micro-engineering laboratory' that would design watches with a rotating cast of freelance talents.

The first piece, Horological Machine N°1 (2007), with its figure-eight case and four barrels, set the tone. It was followed by the HM2, the dome-eyed HM3 and its 'Frog' version, the jet-inspired HM4 Thunderbolt, the Space Pirate HM6 and the jellyfish-like HM7 Aquapod. In 2011 the Legacy Machine N°1 introduced a more traditional round line with a flying balance suspended above the dial, a homage to 19th-century watchmaking; the LM Perpetual, developed with Stephen McDonnell, won a GPHG prize.

MB&F opened the M.A.D. Gallery in Geneva in 2011 for mechanical art and later the lower-priced M.A.D. Editions (M.A.D.1 in 2021). The company reported sales of about CHF 45 million in 2023 from 419 MB&F Machines and roughly 3,500 M.A.D. Editions watches.

In August 2024 Chanel acquired a 25% stake, with Büsser keeping 60% and partner Serge Kriknoff 15%. The brand marked its 20th anniversary in 2025 with the LM101 EVO and limited Legacy Machine editions.

name: Greubel Forsey
tagline: Inclined tourbillons and obsessive hand-finishing from La Chaux-de-Fonds
summary: Greubel Forsey was founded in 2004 by Robert Greubel and Stephen Forsey to push the tourbillon and chronometry further, starting with the Double Tourbillon 30°. Its watches, made in roughly 100-200 pieces a year, are benchmarks for hand finishing and among the most expensive regular-production watches in the world.
history:
Alsatian Robert Greubel and Englishman Stephen Forsey met at Renaud et Papi, the complication specialist, and in 2001 set up a development company to explore improving the tourbillon. Their first watch, the Double Tourbillon 30°, debuted at Baselworld 2004 with one tourbillon cage inclined at 30° spinning inside another, averaging out positional errors.

From a small workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds the pair created the EWT (Experimental Watch Technology) research platform and developed the Tourbillon 24 Secondes, the Quadruple Tourbillon with differential, and from 2012 balance-wheel models such as the Double Balancier 35°. The Richemont group took a 20% minority stake in 2006 that the company later bought back. In 2019 its Hand Made 1 - a tourbillon made almost entirely by hand - redefined its artisanal ambitions.

The 2020s brought the Convexe line (Balancier Convexe S², GMT Balancier Convexe) and a change in leadership. CEO Antonio Calce departed in 2024, succeeded by long-time marketing head Michel Nydegger, and in February 2025 ownership was consolidated between the two founders, with Robert Greubel as chairman. Stephen Forsey was later removed from any operational role, while remaining a shareholder.

The company now makes around 200 watches a year from its La Chaux-de-Fonds atelier, with prices ranging from roughly $180,000 to around a million dollars.

name: De Bethune
tagline: Blued titanium, floating lugs and research-driven watchmaking from the Jura
summary: De Bethune is a manufacture in L'Auberson founded in 2002 by David Zanetta and master watchmaker Denis Flageollet. It is known for its space-age design language - flame-blued titanium, starry skies and floating lugs - and for technical research into balances, shock protection and moonphases.
history:
Collector David Zanetta and watchmaker Denis Flageollet, a specialist in restoring antique timepieces, founded De Bethune in 2002 in the Jura village of L'Auberson near Sainte-Croix. The name honours the Chevalier de Béthune, an 18th-century figure credited with an escapement invention. From the start, Flageollet treated the brand as a research laboratory, developing a self-regulating twin barrel, silicon and titanium-platinum balance wheels, a triple 'parachute' shock absorber and a precise spherical moonphase.

The DB28, introduced in 2010 with its articulated floating lugs and open, blued-titanium architecture, became the house's defining silhouette and won the Aiguille d'Or at the 2011 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. Heat-blued titanium dials pierced with white-gold 'stars' - the Starry Varius and Starry Seas pieces - became another signature.

Zanetta sold his majority stake in 2017 after years of financial difficulty, and in 2021 WatchBox (now The 1916 Company) acquired a controlling stake, with Pierre Jacques leading the business for several years before becoming honorary president. Flageollet remains in charge of creative and technical direction.

De Bethune produces only a few hundred watches a year with a team of under a hundred people, making almost every component in-house, and remains one of the most distinctive voices in independent watchmaking.

name: Urwerk
tagline: Satellite hours and wandering time from Geneva's sci-fi watchmakers
summary: Urwerk was founded in Geneva in 1997 by watchmaker Felix Baumgartner and designer Martin Frei. Its watches replace hands with rotating 'satellite' hour cubes and cones that travel across a minute arc, in angular titanium and steel cases inspired by spacecraft.
history:
Felix Baumgartner, the son of a clock restorer, and his brother Thomas teamed up with art-school-trained designer Martin Frei in the mid-1990s. Launched at Baselworld 1997 with the UR-101 and UR-102, their company took its name from the Mesopotamian city of Ur, where early timekeeping began, combined with the German 'Werk' for movement.

The founders reinvented the 17th-century 'wandering hours' display: numerals mounted on rotating satellites sweep along a scale to indicate the minutes. Later pieces added turbine-regulated automatic winding (UR-202), linear displays inspired by an old Patek Philippe prototype (UR-CC1 King Cobra), the Zeit Device pocket watch (UR-1001) and the EMC, whose movement lets owners monitor and adjust its own rate. The UR-210 added a retrograde winding-efficiency indicator; the UR-100V (2019) became the core line; and the UR-150 Scorpion (2023) introduced a retrograde satellite.

Urwerk remains fully independent and led by its founders, producing around 200 watches a year. It also collaborated with MB&F on the C1 clock and with pop-culture projects, and in 2024 revisited its origins with the UR-102 Reloaded set. Its designs, often compared to spacecraft and sci-fi props, made Urwerk one of the defining names of avant-garde independent watchmaking.

name: Laurent Ferrier
tagline: Pebble-smooth cases and classical chronometry from a Patek Philippe veteran
summary: Laurent Ferrier is a Geneva brand founded by a former Patek Philippe watchmaker after 37 years at the firm. Its soft 'Galet' pebble cases, restrained dials and superbly finished micro-rotor and tourbillon calibres have won multiple GPHG prizes.
history:
Laurent Ferrier spent 37 years at Patek Philippe, rising to technical director, while racing cars in his spare time - he finished third overall at the 1979 24 Hours of Le Mans with his friend François Servanin. Servanin later became the financial backer of Ferrier's own brand, which was set up in Geneva with his son Christian Ferrier and launched its first watches in 2010.

The debut Galet Classic Tourbillon Double Spiral, with a discreet tourbillon hidden on the back and a twin-hairspring balance, won the Best Men's Watch prize at the 2010 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. It was followed by the Galet Micro-Rotor with a natural escapement in silicon, the cushion-shaped Galet Square, travel-time and annual calendar models, and the integrated-bracelet Grand Sport Tourbillon Pursuit and Sport Auto.

Servanin, the controlling shareholder, took a hands-on role in the late 2010s. In January 2025 long-serving board member Florent Perrichon was appointed CEO. The manufacture in Plan-les-Ouates produces a few hundred watches a year, and the Classic Moon won the brand's fifth GPHG award in 2024. The brand remains small and family-rooted, prized for restrained design and finishing of the highest order.

name: Czapek
tagline: A 19th-century Geneva name, revived with the backing of its collectors
summary: Czapek & Cie revives the house of François Czapek, the Polish-Czech watchmaker who was Antoni Patek's first partner in Geneva. Relaunched in 2015 with collector crowdfunding, it is known for the Quai des Bergues, the integrated-bracelet Antarctique and inventive dial work.
history:
François Czapek, a Czech-born watchmaker who had fought in the Polish uprising of 1830-31, settled in Geneva and in 1839 co-founded Patek, Czapek & Cie with fellow émigré Antoni Patek. The partnership ended in 1845, when Patek joined Adrien Philippe and Czapek founded his own firm, Czapek & Cie. He supplied watches to European nobility, including Emperor Napoleon III, opened a shop near the Place Vendôme in Paris and published a treatise on watchmaking in 1850. The firm faded after his era.

In 2012 entrepreneur Xavier de Roquemaurel, investor Harry Guhl and watchmaker Sébastien Follonier created a company to revive the name. Instead of a traditional launch, they sold shares to collectors, dubbed 'Fellow Investors', and presented the Quai des Bergues in 2015, inspired by an 1850 Czapek pocket watch. The Faubourg de Cracovie chronograph and Place Vendôme tourbillon followed, with the Place Vendôme Complicité winning a GPHG public prize.

The integrated-bracelet Antarctique (2020) became the brand's commercial breakthrough and spawned rattrapante, tourbillon and smaller 'S' versions. Still led by de Roquemaurel and based in Geneva, Czapek marked its tenth anniversary in 2025.

name: Kari Voutilainen
tagline: Finnish master of guilloché and hand-finishing in the Val-de-Travers
summary: Kari Voutilainen is a Finnish watchmaker working in Môtiers, Switzerland, whose tiny output of hand-finished watches features his own direct-impulse movements and hand-guilloché dials made in-house at Comblémine. He is considered one of the finest living artisan-watchmakers.
history:
Born in Finland in 1962, Kari Voutilainen trained at the Finnish watchmaking school and later at WOSTEP in Switzerland, where he also taught. He worked in the restoration department of Parmigiani Fleurier, specialising in complicated antique pieces, before going independent in 2002 in Môtiers, in the Val-de-Travers.

His first wristwatch series, the Observatoire, was built on vintage chronometer movements with exquisite guilloché dials. In 2011 he introduced the Vingt-8 calibre, featuring a double escape-wheel direct-impulse escapement developed for efficiency and accuracy; it underpinned most of his models, including GMT, moonphase and power-reserve variants, until its retirement at the end of 2025. Later calibres include the KV20 and the tonneau-shaped KV21 with its dual-wheel direct impulse escapement.

To control his supply chain he acquired the dial maker Comblémine in 2014 and co-founded the case maker Voutilainen & Cattin. In 2021 he led an investor group that acquired Urban Jürgensen, serving as co-CEO until stepping back into an advisory role. His workshop makes fewer than 60 watches a year, collaborates with artisans such as Japanese urushi lacquer masters, and has won several GPHG prizes, including in 2025.

name: Philippe Dufour
tagline: The Vallée de Joux master whose Simplicity defined independent watchmaking
summary: Philippe Dufour is a watchmaker from Le Sentier in the Vallée de Joux whose three wristwatches - the Grande Sonnerie, Duality and Simplicity - are regarded as benchmarks of hand-finishing. Made in tiny numbers, they now command seven-figure prices at auction.
history:
Born in 1948 in Le Sentier, Philippe Dufour trained at the Vallée de Joux watchmaking school and worked for Jaeger-LeCoultre, Gérald Genta and Audemars Piguet, including stints abroad teaching and servicing complicated watches. In 1978 he set up his own workshop in Le Sentier, restoring antique pieces and building complicated movements for other houses.

In 1992 he unveiled the first wristwatch with a grande and petite sonnerie with minute repeater, a stunning achievement for a lone artisan, and made only four examples. In 1996 came the Duality, the first wristwatch with two balance wheels linked by a differential, of which only nine were made. His 2000 Simplicity, a time-only watch with small seconds and an obsessively hand-finished movement, was produced in about 200 examples (in 34mm and 37mm) and became the archetypal collector's grail of the independent movement.

Dufour largely stopped serial production in the 2010s, though a 20th-anniversary Simplicity series was delivered in the early 2020s and he continues to make occasional unique pieces for charity. His influence on younger independents - through mentoring and his insistence on traditional hand-finishing - is immense, and his watches regularly sell for well over a million dollars.

name: Ressence
tagline: Belgian design-led watches that tell time with rotating discs, not hands
summary: Ressence is a Belgian brand founded in Antwerp in 2010 by industrial designer Benoît Mintiens. Its patented ROCS system displays time on orbiting, convex discs, and oil-filled models like the Type 3 make the display look printed on the crystal.
history:
Benoît Mintiens, an industrial designer who had worked on products from trains to consumer goods, founded Ressence in Antwerp in 2010. The name blends 'renaissance' and 'essence'. The ZeroSeries (Type 1001) debuted at Baselworld 2010, introducing a dial with no conventional hands: instead, a set of discs and sub-discs rotate in orbit around one another, driven by a module mounted on a modified Swiss automatic base.

The system, later called ROCS (Ressence Orbital Convex System), evolved through the Type 1 and, in 2013, the Type 3, whose upper chamber is filled with oil. The fluid eliminates internal reflection so the dial seems to sit on the surface of the crystal; the Type 3 won the Horological Revelation prize at the 2013 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. The oil-filled Type 5 diver (2015) stayed legible underwater at any angle, and the cushion-cased Type 1 Squared followed in 2017. Early models had no crown at all, being set and wound through a rotating caseback lever.

Later innovations included the Type 2 with its e-Crown electromechanical setting system, the minimalist Type 8, and collaborations such as a Type 3 with designer Marc Newson. The company, headquartered in Antwerp, remains an independent, design-led outlier in a Swiss-dominated field.

name: Armin Strom
tagline: Biel manufacture pioneering twin-balance resonance in the wristwatch
summary: Armin Strom is a Biel-based manufacture that grew from a renowned skeletonising workshop into an independent maker of in-house movements. It is best known for its patented resonance clutch spring, which couples two balance wheels, and for its openly displayed, off-centre dials.
history:
Armin Strom, a watchmaker from Burgdorf, established his business in 1967 and became celebrated for hand-skeletonised watches, engraving and openworking movements from other makers into delicate lacework. In 2006 the brand was taken over by investors including Willy Michel and his son Serge Michel, with master watchmaker Claude Greisler joining as technical lead; the founder retired.

The new owners transformed Armin Strom into a manufacture in Biel, launching their first in-house calibre around 2009 and building a large proportion of components themselves. The brand's signature became visible mechanics: dials pushed off-centre so that barrels, wheels and balances are on display on the front of the watch.

In 2016 the Mirrored Force Resonance introduced a patented clutch spring that links two independent balance wheels so they synchronise through resonance, improving stability. The resonance platform expanded into a dual time GMT and, in 2020, a minute repeater. More recently the System78 line - including the Tribute, Orbit with on-demand date and the Gravity Equal Force with a patented equal-force barrel - aimed at more accessible haute horlogerie.

Today Armin Strom is owned and run by Serge Michel and Claude Greisler and produces a few hundred watches a year in Biel.

name: Louis Moinet
tagline: Honouring the inventor of the chronograph with meteorites and tourbillons
summary: Ateliers Louis Moinet is a Saint-Blaise brand created in 2004 by Jean-Marie Schaller to honour Louis Moinet, the French horologist whose 1816 'compteur de tierces' is recognised as the first chronograph. It is known for limited, highly decorative pieces using meteorites and rare stones, and for the Memoris chronograph.
history:
Louis Moinet (1768-1853), born in Bourges, was a painter, sculptor and professor of fine arts at the Louvre as well as a gifted horologist and collaborator of Abraham-Louis Breguet. In 1815-1816 he built the 'compteur de tierces', an instrument measuring sixtieths of a second at 216,000 vibrations per hour for astronomical observation - now recognised as the first chronograph. He made clocks for Napoleon, Thomas Jefferson and James Monroe, and in 1848 published a celebrated two-volume Traité d'Horlogerie.

In 2004 Jean-Marie Schaller, a watch industry executive, founded Ateliers Louis Moinet in Saint-Blaise near Neuchâtel to revive the name. The brand became known for tiny limited series with exotic materials - meteorite, lunar and Martian rock, dinosaur bone, rare minerals - and for complex tourbillons. When the original compteur de tierces resurfaced, it was authenticated and presented by the brand, earning Guinness World Records recognition as the first chronograph.

For the bicentenary, the brand launched the Memoris (2015), billed as the first watch built around a chronograph displayed on the dial side. Later creations include the Space Revolution with twin satellite tourbillons and meteorite fragments, and space- and astronomy-themed 'Cosmic Art' pieces. Louis Moinet produces small quantities of limited editions and bespoke pieces from Saint-Blaise.

name: Speake-Marin
tagline: English-founded Geneva independent known for the Piccadilly case and heart-shaped hands
summary: Speake-Marin was founded in 2002 by English watchmaker Peter Speake-Marin and is now run from Geneva under CEO Christelle Rosnoblet. It is recognised by its stepped Piccadilly case, heart-shaped 'topping tool' hands, and in-house micro-rotor calibres, with the Ripples integrated sports watch as its modern hit.
history:
Peter Speake-Marin trained in England and cut his teeth restoring antique watches at a firm in London's Piccadilly, then moved to Switzerland, where he worked at complication specialist Renaud et Papi. In 2002 he launched his own brand in Bursins, Vaud, with the Piccadilly, a watch with a distinctive stepped case and hands whose heart-shaped tips were inspired by a watchmaker's topping tool.

The brand developed its in-house SM2 calibre around 2009 for the Marin 1, and later produced tourbillons, minute repeaters and the Renaissance minute-repeater tourbillon, while Speake-Marin himself consulted for houses such as Harry Winston, MB&F and Maîtres du Temps. In 2017 the founder left the company that bore his name; Christelle Rosnoblet, an administrator since 2012, became CEO, and the headquarters moved to Geneva in 2019.

Under the new leadership the brand broadened its range with the Ripples integrated-bracelet sports watch, the Openworked collection with sandblasted skeletonised movements, and the Piccadilly-cased Resilience with grand feu enamel dials, powered by the in-house SMA03 micro-rotor calibre. The atelier says thirteen manufacture movements have been developed over its history. Its heart-shaped hands and stepped case remain the brand's most recognisable signatures.

name: Akrivia (Rexhep Rexhepi)
tagline: A Kosovo-born prodigy's Geneva atelier, making modern chronometers by hand
summary: Atelier Akrivia, now presented under its founder's name Rexhep Rexhepi, was founded in Geneva in 2012. Its Chronomètre Contemporain won the GPHG Men's Watch prize in 2018, and its successor won again in 2022, making Rexhepi one of the most sought-after independents of his generation.
history:
Rexhep Rexhepi was born in Kosovo and moved to Switzerland at age 11. At 15 he began a five-year apprenticeship at Patek Philippe, then worked with several leading Geneva watchmakers before founding his own atelier in 2012, aged 25. He named it Akrivia, from the Greek word for precision.

The first watch, the AK-01 Tourbillon Monopusher Chronograph (2013), was followed by further tourbillon pieces including a chiming jump hour and regulator, and the AK-06, the first Akrivia without a tourbillon. The breakthrough came in 2018 with the Chronomètre Contemporain, a time-only watch with a white grand feu enamel dial, a hand-finished in-house movement and a case by Jean-Pierre Hagmann; it won the GPHG Men's Watch prize. The Chronomètre Contemporain II, with dead-beat seconds and twin barrels, won the same prize in 2022.

The atelier moved to Geneva's Old Town in 2017 and has gradually brought micromechanics (2019), leatherwork (2023) and grand feu enamelling (2024) in-house. A collaboration with Louis Vuitton produced the LVRR-01, and the brand now presents itself under Rexhep Rexhepi's own name. Production is tiny and demand vastly exceeds supply.

name: Romain Gauthier
tagline: Vallée de Joux precision engineer turned maker of constant-force masterpieces
summary: Romain Gauthier is a Le Sentier manufacture founded by a Vallée de Joux-born precision engineer. Its Logical One, with a chain-and-snail-cam constant-force system, and the hand-finished Insight Micro-Rotor and C by Romain Gauthier have made it a respected technical independent, with Chanel as a minority shareholder.
history:
Born in the Vallée de Joux in 1975, Romain Gauthier trained in precision mechanics and worked in the region's component industry, including programming CNC machines for high-end movement parts, before studying business. In 2002 he set up his own company in Le Sentier, initially making components for other brands, while developing his own watches.

His first watch, the Prestige HM with an in-house movement, arrived in the mid-2000s and was followed by the Prestige HMS in 2012. In 2013 he launched the Logical One, which re-imagined the fusée-and-chain constant-force system with a compact snail-shaped cam and a ruby-link chain, earning GPHG recognition and becoming the brand's signature.

Chanel acquired a minority stake in the company, one of its first moves into independent watchmaking, while Gauthier kept control. Later models included the Insight Micro-Rotor, with an off-centre dial and extensive hand finishing, and in 2021 C by Romain Gauthier, a sportier titanium watch with an integrated bracelet. The manufacture, still based in Le Sentier, produces a few hundred watches a year and also designs mechanical objets such as cufflinks. The brand is a member of the Fondation de la Haute Horlogerie and continues to refine its three core collections: Logical One, Insight and C.

name: Andersen Genève
tagline: Geneva's world-time specialist, founded by an AHCI co-founder
summary: Andersen Genève was founded in 1980 by Danish watchmaker Svend Andersen, a co-founder of the AHCI. Making around 50 watches a year, it is best known for its ultra-thin world-time watches, jumping hours and Montre à Tact.
history:
Danish-born Svend Andersen trained in Denmark and moved to Switzerland, where he worked in the complications workshop of Patek Philippe in Geneva for several years. In 1980 he went independent, opening his own atelier in Geneva, and in 1985 he co-founded the Académie Horlogère des Créateurs Indépendants (AHCI) with Vincent Calabrese to support independent watchmakers.

Andersen became renowned for reviving the world-time complication pioneered by Louis Cottier, making ultra-thin world-time modules at a time when few houses offered the function. He also made unusual complications and one-off pieces, from secular calendars to discreet erotic automata, earning the nickname 'watchmaker of the impossible'.

Today Andersen Genève operates from a riverside atelier in Geneva and a case workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds, producing about 50 watches a year across its World Timer collection (Tempus Terrae, Rattrapante Mondiale, Communication 45), Jumping Hours and Montre à Tact lines, with many pieces customised with enamel, stone and hand-engraved dials. The brand celebrated its 45th anniversary in 2025. Many Andersen pieces are one-offs or tiny series made to a client's wishes, with dials in materials ranging from jade to grand feu enamel, reflecting a lineage of pure artisanal watchmaking.

name: Christophe Claret
tagline: Le Locle complications master behind gaming watches and chiming tourbillons
summary: Christophe Claret is a Le Locle manufacture that for two decades built complex movements - minute repeaters, tourbillons, chronographs - for major brands before launching its own watches in 2009. Its own-name pieces range from Westminster-chiming tourbillons to watches that play blackjack or roulette.
history:
Born in Lyon in 1962, Christophe Claret trained in watchmaking in Geneva and worked restoring antique pieces before founding his own company in 1989, initially specialising in minute repeaters and other complications for leading Swiss brands. The business grew into a sizeable complications manufacture and moved into the Château du Soleil d'Or in Le Locle, a 19th-century manor that houses its workshops.

In 2009, marking 20 years in business, Claret launched watches under his own name with the DualTow. A series of spectacular pieces followed: the 21 Blackjack and other gaming watches with playable mechanisms, the Soprano tourbillon minute repeater with a Westminster chime, the X-TREM-1 with hours and minutes shown by magnetically driven floating steel balls, the Kantharos chronograph, the Maestoso with a detent escapement, and the Margot, a women's watch that plays 'loves me, loves me not'.

The company continues to develop and produce complications for other houses alongside its own low-volume collections, and remains owned by its founder. Its own-brand watches are made in very small numbers and are among the most mechanically ambitious playful watches of the modern era.

name: Konstantin Chaykin
tagline: Russia's inventor-watchmaker, from the Joker Wristmon to the world's thinnest watch
summary: Konstantin Chaykin is a Moscow-based watchmaker and inventor who founded his workshop in 2003 and became the first Russian member of the AHCI. He is known for playful 'Wristmon' faces like the Joker, astronomical complications, and the record-breaking 1.65mm ThinKing.
history:
Born in St Petersburg in 1975, Konstantin Chaykin came to watchmaking via antiques and restoration and set up his independent workshop in 2003. He completed his first clock in 2004 and specialised early in astronomical and calendar mechanisms, including clocks that compute the date of Orthodox Easter; his first patent, for an Easter date indicator, was granted in 2007.

In 2010 he became the first and only Russian member of the Académie Horlogère des Créateurs Indépendants, later serving as its president from 2016 to 2019. He moved production to Moscow in 2012. His watches include the Lunokhod with a spherical moonphase (2011), the Cinema with a mechanical cinematograph animation (2013), the single-hand Genius Temporis (2014) and the Mars Conqueror series telling Martian time.

In 2017 he created the Joker, the first of his 'Wristmons' - watches whose dials form faces, with hours and minutes as eyes and a moonphase as a grinning mouth - which became his best-known design. In 2020 he received the WIPO Medal for Inventors, and he holds over 100 patents. In 2024 he unveiled the ThinKing, a mechanical watch just 1.65mm thick, claiming the title of the world's thinnest.

name: Grönefeld
tagline: Dutch brothers building Swiss-grade constant-force watches in Oldenzaal
summary: Grönefeld is a Dutch independent run by brothers Bart and Tim Grönefeld in Oldenzaal, where their family has worked in horology since 1912. Their 1941 Remontoire and 1941 Grönograaf both won GPHG awards.
history:
The Grönefeld family's horological roots go back to 1912, when the brothers' grandfather established a watch and clock business in Oldenzaal in the east of the Netherlands. Bart and Tim Grönefeld trained at WOSTEP in Switzerland and then worked for years at Renaud et Papi (later Audemars Piguet Renaud & Papi), specialising in grand complications and tourbillons.

In 2008 the brothers launched watches under the Grönefeld name, producing complex pieces such as the Parallax Tourbillon and the dead-beat-seconds One Hertz, all assembled and finished in Oldenzaal. The 1941 Remontoire, introduced in 2016 with an eight-second constant-force remontoir, won the Men's Watch prize at the 2016 GPHG. The automatic 1941 Principia followed, and in 2022 the 1941 Grönograaf chronograph won another GPHG prize.

The brothers are AHCI members and produce very small numbers of watches; demand has at times been so high that the workshop has stopped accepting new orders. Recent designs include the 1969 DeltaWorks and the women's 1944 Tanfana. Everything from design to final hand-finishing is done in the family workshop, in the same town where the family business began more than a century ago.

name: Habring²
tagline: Austrian husband-and-wife manufacture making honest complications by hand
summary: Habring² is a small Austrian manufacture founded in 2004 by Richard and Maria Kristina Habring in Carinthia. Known for affordable-by-independent-standards watches with in-house movements, it specialises in split-seconds chronographs, dead-beat (jumping) seconds and foudroyante complications.
history:
Richard Habring trained in Austria and spent years at IWC in Schaffhausen, where he worked on complications including the brand's split-seconds chronograph development. With his wife Maria Kristina he set up an independent workshop, and in 2004 the couple launched Habring² - the squared symbol representing the two of them - in Völkermarkt, Carinthia.

The Habrings built a reputation for mechanically serious watches at comparatively modest prices, often modifying and then replacing base calibres with their own construction. Their range includes the split-seconds chronograph Doppel, the jumping-seconds Erwin, the Foudroyante-Felix with a flying one-eighth-second display, and the time-only Felix, powered by their in-house A11 calibre.

The company remains a small family business with a handful of watchmakers, producing watches largely to order with extensive customisation. It marked its 20th anniversary in 2024 with the Oskar and Josef models, and continues to be one of the most respected value propositions in independent watchmaking. Customers can specify dial colours, numerals, hands and case details, and many watches are assembled only after an order is placed. The small team handles design, movement production, finishing and service under one roof.

name: MING
tagline: Design-first watches from photographer Ming Thein's collector-founded brand
summary: MING was founded in 2017 by photographer and designer Ming Thein with a group of watch-enthusiast friends. Known for layered sapphire dials, inventive lume and quick-change straps at accessible prices, its 37.09 Bluefin won the Sports Watch Prize at the 2024 GPHG.
history:
Ming Thein, a Malaysian photographer, designer and watch collector, launched MING in 2017 together with a small group of fellow collectors. The idea was a design-first brand that would use high-quality Swiss-made components and movements while pushing aesthetics through unusual materials, layered and textured sapphire dials and distinctive luminous treatments.

The first model, the 17.01, sold out quickly and set the template: tightly controlled limited editions, often sold in online drops, with prices well below traditional Swiss independents. Later lines included chronographs, a hand-wound 'monopusher' range, and more complex pieces made with partners such as Schwarz Etienne and J.N. Shapiro. The brand operates as Horologer MING, a Swiss watchmaker, with a globally distributed team.

MING's 37-series dive and sports watches brought the brand to a wider public: the 37.09 Bluefin, a 600m diver with lume embedded in its sapphire, won the Sports Watch Prize at the 2024 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. Recent releases include the 37.11 Odyssey GMT and the 57.05 Comet worldtimer. The brand has built an unusually engaged online community, and its limited editions typically sell out quickly, with deliveries planned in batches. Its watches pair Swiss-made Sellita-based or partner movements with in-house design.

name: Petermann Bédat
tagline: Two young Vaud watchmakers reviving dead-beat seconds and rattrapantes
summary: Petermann Bédat is an independent atelier in Renens near Lausanne founded by Gaël Petermann and Florian Bédat, who met at the Geneva watchmaking school. Its hand-finished Reference 1967 dead-beat seconds and Reference 2941 monopusher split-seconds chronograph are made in editions of just ten.
history:
Gaël Petermann and Florian Bédat met as students at the Geneva watchmaking school and went on to work in Switzerland and Germany, including in restoration and haute horlogerie workshops, before joining forces to create their own atelier in Renens, near Lausanne.

Their first watch, the Reference 1967, arrived in 2018: a dead-beat seconds wristwatch with an in-house calibre, inspired by pocket-watch architecture and German-school finishing, with a semi-open sapphire dial ringed in sandblasted steel. It was made in only ten pieces each in rose and white gold and quickly made them names to watch among collectors.

They followed with the Reference 2941, a platinum monopusher split-seconds chronograph with a jumping minute counter and their Calibre 202, again limited to ten pieces, and more recently the Reference 1825, a purist three-hand watch with a redesigned calibre. The pair continue to hand-finish every component in their small workshop. Their approach favours small, hand-made batches over growth: each watch is assembled, finished and regulated in-house, with traditional techniques such as bevelling, perlage and Côtes de Genève applied by hand. Collectors have embraced them as leading representatives of a new generation of Swiss independents.

name: Simon Brette
tagline: A French engineer's marine-chronometer-inspired debut from Geneva
summary: Simon Brette is a Geneva-based independent founded in 2021 by a French engineer who previously designed movements at Chronode, MCT and MB&F. His Chronomètre Artisans, with a hand-engraved red-gold dial and slow 2.5Hz beat, was launched through a collector subscription edition.
history:
Simon Brette, the son of a carpenter, trained as an engineer and worked as a technical designer and movement constructor at Chronode, MCT and MB&F, contributing to some of the most unconventional mechanisms of the 2010s. In 2021 he set up his own brand in Geneva.

His first watch, the Chronomètre Artisans, was presented in 2023. Drawing on marine chronometers, its proprietary calibre SBCA beats at a slow 2.5Hz and runs for 72 hours on twin barrels. The dial combines a 5N red-gold base hand-engraved with a 'dragon scale' motif, translucent sapphire plates for the minutes and seconds, and an observatory-style hour hand inspired by English watchmaker Derek Pratt.

To fund development, Brette offered a Subscription Edition of just 12 pieces in zirconium to early backers, which sold out at around CHF 50,000 each before a regular production edition in traditional case metals followed. The debut was widely praised as one of the most accomplished first watches by a young independent. He continues to develop the brand from Geneva with a small team, favouring traditional hand-engraving and finishing. Case, dial and movement are all his own designs.

name: Cyrus
tagline: Le Locle-made avant-garde complications, led by the Klepcys
summary: Cyrus is a Swiss independent with headquarters in Plan-les-Ouates and a manufacture in Le Locle, owned by Dr. Pablo Richard with master watchmaker Jean-François Mojon. It is known for the Klepcys family of bold, complicated watches featuring vertical tourbillons, retrograde GMTs and unusual hour displays.
history:
Cyrus positions itself as an avant-garde manufacture emphasising technical independence. Its watches are produced in Le Locle with the involvement of master watchmaker Jean-François Mojon, a well-known complications specialist, while the company's headquarters are in Plan-les-Ouates near Geneva. The business is owned and presided over by Dr. Pablo Richard.

The brand's signature collection is the Klepcys, whose name evokes the clepsydra, an ancient water clock. Klepcys models combine an architectural case with complicated displays: the Klepcys Vertical Tourbillon, limited to 38 pieces per version in rose gold and black DLC titanium; the Klepcys GMT Retrograde; the Klepcys Réveil alarm; and the Klepcys DICE, issued in titanium editions of 50 pieces. The Dominion GMT and the Etheral Twin Orbital Tourbillon broaden the range.

Cyrus produces small limited series and remains a niche name even among collectors of independent watchmaking. Its limited editions are distributed through a small network of retailers and directly by the company. The brand combines contemporary materials such as black DLC titanium with traditional complications, and its modular approach allows the Klepcys case to host very different mechanisms, from alarms to tourbillons. Its catalogue currently lists around seventeen references across its collections.
